claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 at% Y to the WMoTaNbV alloy with minor Al will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The initial material is a WMoTaNbV-based refractory high-entropy alloy containing minor Al and no Y.
The intervention is introduction of approximately 0.5 at% Y during alloy synthesis.
The Y-modified alloy will form a continuous and adherent Y-rich Al2O3 surface scale.
Y segregates to the oxide/alloy interface at high temperature.
Interfacial Y promotes nucleation and growth of a thermodynamically stable, protective Al2O3 scale.
The reactive-element effect of Y reduces oxide-growth stresses.
The Y-promoted protective scale inhibits inward diffusion of oxygen.
At 1200°C in air for 100 hours, the Y-doped alloy will have significantly lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated alloy.
At 1200°C in air for 100 hours, the Y-doped alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy has faster oxidation kinetics and higher weight gain at 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
The untreated alloy undergoes oxide-scale spallation at 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
The expected improvement is limited to constant isothermal exposure at 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
Performance at other temperatures or under cyclic thermal exposure is undetermined.
The magnitude of oxidation improvement depends on Y concentration and segregation behavior.
Unoptimized Y doping could adversely affect phase stability or mechanical properties.
Comparing untreated and approximately 0.5 at% Y-doped samples under identical isothermal oxidation conditions can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight gain or improvement in oxide-scale integrity in the Y-doped alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
